newsitem.title: UK: Winter demand boosts oil, but outlook uncertain.
newsitem.headline: Winter demand boosts oil, but outlook uncertain.

text.p: Winter demand for heating oil products in the United States and Europe fuelled a rise in world oil prices on Friday.
The rally was capped by concerns over the effect rising production might have on global stocks over the next few months, traders and analysts said.

Benchmark Brent Blend crude oil for December delivery on the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) closed 77 cents higher at $22.98 a barrel on Friday after failing to break through the intra-day high of $23.00 a barrel.
Brokers said the move up came in a late short-covering scramble in very low volume and could not be seen as a definite signal prices were consolidating higher.
Gas oil (European heating oil) also rose early before easing from the highs. It closed $1 a tonne higher at $222 a tonne.
Gas oil has risen by $16, or eight percent, from lows to highs this week, helped by winter demand and the strength of the Far Eastern market.
And a tussle between two trading companies battling for control of the November IPE gas oil contract before it expires next week is fanning the flames further, traders said.

But product and crude markets are likely to struggle to regain the highs hit in October over the coming weeks as refineries in the United States and Europe work flat out to replenish dwindling stocks of heating oil, they added.

Crude oil prices hit their highest level since the 1991 Gulf War of $25.06 a barrel about a month ago amid Middle East tensions, buoyant demand and fears that low heating oil stocks would fall short during the winter.
Unless the winter is exceptionally cold, inventories should return to more normal levels.

"From the second quarter 1997, we see a constant build on stocks. I think the market will take note early on so any price spike will be sold into," said Mohammed Abduljabbar, oil consultant at Petroleum Finance Corp.

The market shook off the latest forecasts from the International Energy (IEA), which projected world oil demand of 73.8 million barrels per day (bpd) during the fourth quarter of 1996, up 1.9 million barrels from year-ago levels.
Traders noted that the Paris-based agency also forecast that the stock shortfall is expected to "decrease appreciably" during the last three months of the year as non-OPEC supply grew.
